transcript.text: Good morning, everyone. Thanks for making time for this round-robin check-in. As we discuss the peer-feedback pilot proposal, I want to make sure we're all aligned on the operating safeguards before I issue the final plan. The proposal currently covers facilitated discussion, ordinary participation, and a review after the pilot — but the detailed safeguards still need to be defined. Let's hear from each of you on what you think those safeguards should include.
transcript.speaker: A1

transcript.text: I want to flag something I've personally observed. Across the last three retrospectives, I counted exactly five dismissive interruptions. On top of that, two colleagues separately told me they'd rather contribute only through an anonymous written channel than speak up in the group. I think our safeguards need to account for this pattern of interruption and the real reluctance some people feel about speaking openly.

transcript.text: I need to share something important that hasn't made it into the proposal yet. I confirmed with HR this morning that because this pilot follows repeated conduct concerns, specific safeguards are required: the pilot must be opt-in, it must use an independent neutral facilitator, participants must sign a written non-retaliation acknowledgment, and there must be a documented review exactly 30 days after launch. The HR guidance came in after the current draft circulated, so these details weren't captured in the version you've all been looking at. I think these need to be incorporated into the final plan before Elena issues it.

transcript.text: Thank you both for these critical inputs. Darius, the pattern you've observed — five dismissive interruptions across three retrospectives and two colleagues preferring anonymous written channels — is exactly the kind of ground-level evidence we need to design safeguards that actually work. I'm taking that seriously. Mei, the HR guidance you're describing changes the picture significantly. The requirements of opt-in participation, an independent neutral facilitator, a signed non-retaliation acknowledgment, and a documented review at exactly 30 days post-launch are not optional — they need to be in the final plan. Let me ask a clarifying question before I settle: Darius, given what you've observed about reluctance to speak up, do you see any tension between the opt-in model and getting enough participation for the pilot to produce meaningful data? And Mei, can you confirm whether the 30-day review replaces or supplements the end-of-pilot review already described in the proposal?
transcript.speaker: A1

transcript.text: Thanks, Elena. To your question about the opt-in model and meaningful participation — I do see a real tension. The two colleagues who told me they'd only contribute through an anonymous written channel are exactly the people whose perspectives we need most, since they've experienced or witnessed the dismissive interruptions that make open discussion feel unsafe. If the pilot is purely opt-in and relies on people voluntarily stepping into a facilitated discussion, I worry we'll mostly hear from those who are already comfortable speaking up, and the pattern I observed could simply reproduce itself. I'd suggest two things: first, offer the anonymous written channel as a parallel input method alongside the facilitated discussion, so people who are reluctant can still participate without being exposed. Second, make it very clear in the opt-in framing that choosing the anonymous written channel counts as full participation — not a lesser form of it. That way we capture meaningful data from the full range of experience, not just from those who feel safe enough to speak in the room.

My understanding is that this serves as a formal checkpoint during the pilot, not a replacement for the end-of-pilot review already in the proposal. The 30-day review is a safeguard to catch issues early — given that this pilot follows repeated conduct concerns, HR wants to ensure problems are identified and addressed mid-course rather than waiting until the full pilot concludes. So the final plan should include both: the 30-day review as a required interim checkpoint, and the existing end-of-pilot review as the concluding assessment. Both should be documented. I'd also note that Darius's suggestion about the anonymous written channel as a parallel input method is worth incorporating — it directly addresses the participation tension he identified while still respecting the opt-in requirement from HR.

commitments.detail: Participation is strictly opt-in; no one is required to join the facilitated discussion.
An independent neutral facilitator will be engaged to run all facilitated sessions.
All participants must sign a written non-retaliation acknowledgment before participating.
A documented interim review will be conducted exactly 30 days after launch to catch issues mid-course.
The existing end-of-pilot review described in the original proposal will be retained as the concluding assessment.
An anonymous written channel will be offered as a parallel input method alongside the facilitated discussion, and it will be explicitly framed as full participation — not a lesser form of it.
The five observed dismissive interruptions across the last three retrospectives will be logged as context for the facilitator, who will be briefed on this pattern.
